title: Label-free Single Molecule Detection Using Microtoroid Optical Resonators
protocol: Fabricate microtoroids using lithography, etching, and melting procedure.
Create microtoroids with a major diameter of 80-100 µm and minor diameter of 2 µm on a silicon wafer.
Unwind approximately one meter of single-mode optical fiber from its spool.
Strip a 2.5 cm segment of polymer coating around the optical fiber using wire strippers.
Clean the stripped portion of the optical fiber with isopropanol alcohol and a lint-free wipe.
Hold the cleaned fiber segment in place using magnetic clamps.
Thin the stripped fiber to approximately 500 nm by melting and pulling with a hydrogen torch and stepper motors moving at 60 µm/min.
Position the optical fiber inside the flame top portion, which is about 10 mm tall.
Stop pulling when the transmission through the fiber ceases fluctuating.
Cleave one end of the optical fiber.
Insert the cleaved end into a bare fiber adaptor.
Place the adapted end of the fiber into the input of the photoreceiver.
Fiber couple the other end of the fiber spool to the laser using a fiber optic coupler.
Mount the microtoroid chip on top of a sample holder using either epoxy or double-sided tape.
Position the sample holder on top of a 3-axis nano-positioning stage.
Coarse position the sample chip using the 3-axis micrometer.
Align the microtoroid-containing chip parallel to the optical fiber using the nano-positioner.
Ensure alignment is within one wavelength of the input light (~633 nm).
Use two imaging columns for visualization, positioned on top and on the side of the chip.
Optimize the polarization of the laser light directed through the optical fiber using an in-line polarization controller.
Adjust the polarization until the measured dip in transmission appears narrowest.
Observe the dip on an oscilloscope.
Construct a sample chamber by epoxying a glass coverslip over the sample stage using a glass microscope slide as a spacer.
Thermally equilibrate particle suspensions or single-molecule aqueous solutions for ≥ 1 hr in a RT water bath (~500 ml).
Vortex particle containing solutions (1 ml) briefly for ~2 sec.
Inject particle containing solutions into the sample chamber at 1 ml/min using a 1 ml syringe pump.
Wait 30 sec before recording data to minimize the effects of mechanical vibrations resulting from fluid flow that can affect the measurement.
Re-couple the toroid to the optical fiber by moving the sample holder with the nanopositioner.
Scan the computer-controlled input laser through various wavelengths using a triangular waveform voltage signal sent to the piezoelectric element in the laser controller.
Perform experiments with visible light at 635 nm ± 2.5 nm due to low water absorption.
Measure light transmission through the optical fiber by connecting its output to an auto-balanced photoreceiver.
Plug the photoreceiver's output into an oscilloscope using a BNC cable.
Observe on the oscilloscope that transmission drops at the resonance wavelength of the microtoroid.
Attach the photoreceiver’s output to the main input of the frequency locking feedback controller via a cable.
Run the frequency locking feedback controller in autolock mode using top-of-peak locking with a dither frequency of 2 kHz.
Set proportional-integral-derivative settings using Ziegler-Nichols tuning rules.
Auto-lock the wavelength of the laser to the resonance wavelength of the microtoroid after filling the sample chamber.
Record the output of the feedback controller at 20 kHz using a 24-bit data acquisition card.
Export the recorded data as a text file via data acquisition software.
Fourier transform the exported data in MATLAB.
Low pass filter the data using a "brick-wall" filter with a cutoff at 1 kHz to remove the imposed dither frequency of 2 kHz.

Notch filter the data using a window size of 16 Hz to remove known sources of noise, including 60 Hz electronic line noise and its harmonics, as well as 100 Hz (coming from the laser driver) and its harmonics.
Inverse Fourier transform the data back into the time domain.
Median filter the data using a window size of 1,001 samples.
Locate step changes in the resonance wavelength using the step-finding algorithm of Kerssemakers et al.
Generate histograms of the amplitude of each binding step.
Calculate particle size using Eq. (1).
